Description:
## Overview

In Digano Mahesar, a small village in Miro Khan taluka of Qambar–Shahdadkot District in upper Sindh, stands the darbar of Bhai Waliram, a Nanakpanthi sant remembered locally as a contemporary of the better-documented Vali Vilayat Rai of Kambar and Swami Dharmdas of Larkana. As with much of this cluster of small Sindhi Nanakpanthi shrines, next to nothing has been preserved in published sources about Bhai Waliram's own dates, teachings, or the founding of his darbar.

## Present State

The site is recorded chiefly in Zulfiqar Ali Kalhoro's surveys of Sindh's Nanakpanthi saints, which place Bhai Waliram among a wider constellation of nineteenth- and early-twentieth-century Nanakpanthi teachers of the Larkana country, without further biographical detail. Its precise founding date, architecture, and present congregation remain undocumented pending a dedicated local or gazetteer source, and this entry should be read as a provisional, lightly-sourced record rather than an established history.

A 2018 profile of the region's Nanakpanthi saints for *The Friday Times*, drawing on Kalhoro's fieldwork, names Bhai Waliram directly as "another famous Nanakpanthi saint" and confirms Digano Mahesar village in Miro Khan taluka as the site of his darbar — though, consistent with the gap already noted above, the article gives no dates, no account of an *urs* or festival, and no description of the building itself.

## Bibliography

- Zulfiqar Ali Kalhoro, published surveys of Nanakpanthi saints and shrines of Sindh.
- Zulfiqar Ali Kalhoro, "Nanakpanthi Saints of Sindh," *The Friday Times*, 13 April 2018.
qa_note: This addition rests on a single independently-verified source (Zulfiqar Ali Kalhoro, "Nanakpanthi Saints of Sindh," The Friday Times, 13 April 2018) and has not yet been corroborated. That source confirms Bhai Waliram's Nanakpanthi identity and the village/taluka location but does not itself verify the Qambar–Shahdadkot district attribution already carried in this entry's Description.

Description:
## Overview

Chandragup, a mud volcano rising from the arid coastal hills of Hingol National Park in Lasbela District, is one of the most sacred halting-points on the annual Hinglaj Yatra, the pilgrimage that draws Hindu devotees across the Kirthar and Makran hills to the shrine of Hinglaj Mata. Known devotionally as Baba Chandragup, the cone is venerated as an abode associated with Shiva, and its periodic eruptions of cold, sulphurous mud are read by pilgrims as auspicious signs.

## The Hinglaj Yatra

During the annual four-day Hinglaj Yatra, held each April, pilgrims halt at Chandragup to fast, keep vigil through the night, and make offerings — coconuts, sweets, flags and coins pressed into the soft mud — before resuming their journey onward to the Hinglaj Mata Temple itself, the yatra's principal destination. The mountain's veneration is of unrecorded antiquity, attested only in the living pilgrimage tradition rather than in any dated textual source.

## A Natural Site Within a Devotional Landscape

Unlike most entries in this collection, Chandragup is not a constructed temple but a natural geological feature — one of several mud volcanoes in the Hingol region — whose sanctity derives entirely from its place within the Hinglaj pilgrimage route. It is filed here under "Hindu Temple" for consistency with the dataset's schema, though it is best understood as a sacred halting-place rather than a built shrine.

Press accounts of the pilgrimage add further devotional detail: an image of Shiva marks the volcano's flanks, and pilgrims traditionally ask the god's permission there before continuing on to visit Sati at the Hinglaj Mata shrine itself. The climb to the rim is reported as physically demanding — muddy and steep, with heat and dust causing some pilgrims to slip or faint from exhaustion — and coconuts are thrown into the crater as offerings and to make wishes. Reported attendance at the wider Hinglaj festival has varied sharply by year and source, from "more than 40,000 people" in 2019 to a reported 200,000 pilgrims across three days in 2025, and the standard academic treatment of the pilgrimage, Jürgen Schaflechner's *Hinglaj Devi: Identity, Change, and Solidification at a Hindu Temple in Pakistan* (Oxford University Press, 2018; Pakistan pbk. 2020), describes Hinglaj as "the most influential Hindu pilgrimage site in Pakistan," of which Chandragup is one station.

## Bibliography

- Wikipedia, "Chandragup" and "Hinglaj Yatra."
- Published accounts and photo-documentation of the annual Hinglaj pilgrimage.
- Gulnaz Khan (photographs by Matthieu Paley), "Hindu Pilgrimage in Pakistan," *National Geographic*, 10 January 2019.
- Saleem Shahid, "Thousands attend festival at Hinglaj Mata temple," *Dawn*, 5 May 2025.
- Jürgen Schaflechner, *Hinglaj Devi: Identity, Change, and Solidification at a Hindu Temple in Pakistan* (Oxford University Press; Pakistan pbk. 2020).
qa_note: The research pass surfaced two unresolved conflicts. On the volcano's size: the Express Tribune (2024) gives Chandragup as "330 feet tall and with a diameter of 49 feet," while Dawn (2014) reports the region's mud volcanoes ranging "between 800 to 1,550 feet" in height and gives the crater's diameter as "about 450 feet (137.16 m)" — figures not reconciled here. On pilgrim numbers: National Geographic (2019) reported "more than 40,000 people" at the Hinglaj Yatra, while Dawn (2025) reported "around 200,000 pilgrims" over three days — different years and possibly different counting bases, both reported as found rather than resolved. Separately, the epithet "Baba Chandragup" used in this entry's title and opening line was not corroborated by any of the established-press or academic sources fetched in this research pass; it was traced only to Wikipedia, which in turn cites a source (Times Now, 2024) below this project's reliability bar, and should be treated as unverified pending a stronger citation.

Description:
Darbar-e-Aliya Naqshbandia Ghamkol Sharif lies in a secluded valley a few miles outside the town of Kohat in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, and is among the most important centres of the *Naqshbandi* Sufi order in modern Pakistan. It was founded in 1952 by the Naqshbandi master universally known as *Zinda Pir* (1912–1999), who was born in the nearby village of Jungle Khail. He had received spiritual authority (*khilafat*) around 1942 from his own guide, Baba Ji Muhammad Qasim of Mohra Sharif, who directed him to establish an independent centre; obedient to that instruction, Zinda Pir withdrew to the then-barren Ghamkol valley and there built, over the following decades, a great complex of mosque, seminary, and lodgings that grew into a thriving spiritual township. His following spread far beyond Pakistan, and the darbar developed an especially strong connection with the Pakistani community of Birmingham in the United Kingdom, where an associated mosque bears its name. Zinda Pir died on 21 March 1999 and is buried at the darbar, his tomb becoming a place of pilgrimage in its turn; his spiritual seat passed to his son, Pir Sayyid Badshah. Each year vast crowds of devotees gather at Ghamkol Sharif for the commemorative observances, making it one of the great living Sufi centres of the north-west.

Independent scholarly confirmation for the core outline comes from the anthropologist Pnina Werbner, who identifies the tariqa's specific branch name as *tariqa Naqshbandiyya Ghamkolia* and who, by the time of her fieldwork, found Zinda Pir's following grown into "a vast, transnational regional cult, stretching throughout Pakistan to the Gulf, Britain, Afghanistan and Southern Africa." She describes the lodge's daily rhythm — "truckloads of supplicants" arriving to seek the saint's blessing, swelling to "a veritable flood" on Fridays, holidays, and the *urs* — and the centrality of the *langar*, through which visitors are fed rather than asked for payment. Her fuller academic account appears in *Pilgrims of Love: The Anthropology of a Global Sufi Cult* (Hurst, 2004; Indiana University Press ed., 2016), the standard scholarly treatment of the darbar and its founder — though her 2009 conference paper on the subject dates the founding of the cult centre to 1948 rather than the 1952 given above, a discrepancy this entry has not resolved.

## Bibliography

- Pnina Werbner, "Transnationalism and Regional Cults: The Dialectics of Sufism in the Plurivocal Muslim World" (conference paper, Keele University, May 2009).
- Pnina Werbner, *Pilgrims of Love: The Anthropology of a Global Sufi Cult* (Hurst, 2004; Indiana University Press ed., 2016).
qa_note: The research pass surfaced a conflict on this darbar's founding date: this entry's Description states 1952, which matches the affiliated UK mosque and charity's own account (Central Jamia Mosque Ghamkol Sharif, "Our Roots," gsmosque.org: "The roots of our Charity, go back as far as 1952"), but Pnina Werbner's 2009 academic conference paper instead dates Zinda Pir's seclusion and the founding of the cult centre to 1948 ("He had founded the cult centre in 1948, when he first secluded himself, according to the legend, in a cave on the hill of Ghamkol"). Neither source is reconciled here.

Description:
The Gori Temple — *Gori jo Mandar*, the "temple of Gori" — is a marble *Śvetāmbara Jain* temple standing amid the desert near the village of Gori, between Islamkot and Nagarparkar in Tharparkar District, some fourteen miles north-west of the Viravah ruins. Built in 1375-1376 CE and dedicated to *Parshvanatha*, the twenty-third *Tirthankara* of the Jain faith, it is one of the most important surviving Jain monuments of the subcontinent's north-west. The temple, raised on a high stepped platform and built of marble, measures roughly 125 by 60 feet and is distinguished by its three *mandapas* (halls) and its remarkable array of some fifty-two domes, whose form blends Gujarati temple design with the regional architecture of the age. Its greatest treasure is its painting: the frescoes within the main dome — depicting princely processions, palanquins and coaches, riders, and elegantly robed figures in flowing Rajasthani dress — are reckoned to be the oldest surviving Jain frescoes in the northern regions of the subcontinent, a survival of extraordinary rarity. Long abandoned as a place of worship, the temple stands today as a monument of the once-flourishing Jain and Hindu culture of the Thar. It forms part of the group of Nagarparkar temples inscribed in 2016 on the UNESCO tentative list as the "Nagarparkar Cultural Landscape," and it remains a site of pilgrimage interest for Jains and Hindus and of growing concern for heritage conservation.

A heritage-preservation survey by the Endowment Fund Trust for the Heritage of Sindh records the temple's main structure as built of a Jodhpuri stone "much like marble," and notes that its last major repairs are recorded to have been carried out in 1715, attributing the damage the temple has suffered over the centuries to Sindhi troops, fire, and gunpowder rather than to the earthquake and British demolition reported elsewhere. Press coverage in 2016 has independently repeated the temple's dedication to Parshvanath and dated its construction only to "around the 16th century" — a looser dating than the 1375-1376 CE given above, which this entry has not reconciled with the more specific figure. The site was already known to colonial-era archaeology: Henry Cousens' 1929 survey of Sindh's antiquities indexes "Gori" among its subjects, though its descriptive passage on the temple itself was not retrieved in this research pass.

## Bibliography

- "Gori Temple," Heritage of Sindh (Endowment Fund Trust for Preservation of the Heritage of Sindh), https://heritage.eftsindh.com/districts/tharparkar/gori-temple.php.
- Ema Anis, "Secrets of Thar: A Jain temple, a mosque and a 'magical' well," *Dawn*, 19 February 2016.
- Henry Cousens, *The Antiquities of Sind, with Historical Outline* (Calcutta: Government of India Central Publication Branch, 1929).
qa_note: This addition's verdict is PARTIAL: only two independent sources were verified in this research pass, and this entry's own pre-existing founding date of 1375-1376 CE is not among the facts corroborated here. The research pass surfaced two further unresolved conflicts. On the founding date: no source fetched in this pass supports 1375-1376 CE specifically; the Endowment Fund Trust for the Heritage of Sindh gives no date at all, and Dawn (2016) gives only "around the 16th century"; Wikipedia's own article on the temple (used only as an uncited pointer, not verified here) separately carries a legend of construction in 300 CE and itself flags the 1375-1376 CE figure as needing a citation. On the cause of historical damage: the Endowment Fund Trust attributes it to "Sindhi troops," fire, and gunpowder, with repairs recorded in 1715, while Dawn (2016) instead attributes wall destruction to an earthquake and to demolition by the British. Neither conflict is resolved here.

Description:
Gurdwara Baoli Sahib stands in the crowded Dabbi Bazaar at the very heart of the walled city of Lahore, where its precinct once adjoined the Loha, Kesera and Guru bazaars. It commemorates a visit of *Guru Arjan Dev*, the fifth Sikh Guru, to Lahore in 1599. In the tradition preserved by the community, a devotee named *Bhai Chhajju Bhagat*, together with a Pathan merchant, laid a purse of gold *mohars* at the Guru's feet and asked that it be spent for religious purposes; the Guru had a *baoli* — a roofed stepwell — sunk at this spot to provide water for the people of the quarter. The stepwell later suffered in the turbulence of the eighteenth century: it is said to have been filled in and built over during the governorship of Nawab Yahya Khan, at the instigation of Diwan Jaspat Rai. It was rediscovered and restored during the reign of *Maharaja Ranjit Singh*, who in 1834 had a new building raised and a *sarovar* (sacred tank) dug, and the gurdwara passed under the management of the Shiromani Gurdwara Parbandhak Committee in 1927. Today the site is also known as Baoli Bagh, its surroundings laid out as a garden. As a shrine tied to Guru Arjan — the compiler of the *Adi Granth* and the first martyr of the Sikh faith, whose principal Lahore memorial is the Gurdwara Dera Sahib by the Fort — Baoli Sahib is a significant station on the map of Sikh Lahore.

Independent verification substantially corroborates and enriches this account. Iqbal Qaiser's 1998 survey of Sikh shrines gives the same origin story and specifies that the dispute was resolved before the Guru in Samvat 1616, while Majid Sheikh's reporting for *Dawn* fixes the disputed purse at "282 gold mohars" and adds that Maharaja Ranjit Singh's 1834 restoration followed his own recovery from illness after his astrologers advised him to bathe in the baoli's water — corroborated independently by the Department of Archaeology's own 1962 memoir, which further records a mosque as having stood on the site between the Sikh gurus' era and Ranjit Singh's reign, a detail found in neither Qaiser's account nor this entry's own Nawab Yahya Khan narrative, and not reconciled with either here. Sheikh's reporting also adds that it was at Gurdwara Baoli Sahib, not elsewhere in Dabbi Bazaar, that the original Adi Granth manuscript (the Kartarpur *pothi*) was kept in the custody of the Sodhi family, carried in grand procession to the Lahore Fort under Ranjit Singh's patronage, and restored to the Sodhi family after the British annexation of 1849. By 2015 the baoli itself had been reduced to "a mere small opening in an open space," with only a few traditional healers still drawing water from it as the water table fell, and by 2018 the same reporter separately flagged the demolition of the gurdwara structure itself as an unaddressed grievance.

## Bibliography

- Iqbal Qaiser, *Historical Sikh Shrines in Pakistan* (Lahore: Punjabi History Board, 1998), p. 218.
- Majid Sheikh, "Harking back: The magical baolis of Arjan and Dina Nath," *Dawn*, 1 February 2015.
- Majid Sheikh, "Harking back: The connection of Dabbi Bazaar to Kartarpur 'pothi'," *Dawn*, 30 September 2018.
- Khan Mohammad Waliullah Khan, *Sikh Shrines in West Pakistan*, Memoir of the Department of Archaeology in Pakistan No. 3 (Karachi: Department of Archaeology, Government of Pakistan, 1962), entry 3, Plate No. 32.
qa_note: The research pass surfaced three unresolved conflicts. (1) On who filled in the baoli and what stood on the site afterward: Iqbal Qaiser's 1998 survey gives only dates (built Samvat 1616, filled Samvat 1685, restored under Ranjit Singh in Samvat 1891) with no mention of a mosque, while the Department of Archaeology's 1962 memoir states that after the time of Guru Har Gobind the baoli was filled up, the langar khana closed, and a mosque built on the site, which Ranjit Singh had pulled down in 1834 to re-open the baoli. Neither source corroborates this entry's own existing account of the fill-in occurring under Nawab Yahya Khan's governorship at Diwan Jaspat Rai's instigation, which remains outside what this research pass verified. (2) On the construction date: Qaiser (via the source he cites, "Tawarikh-e-Guru Khalsa") dates construction to Samvat 1616, while Dawn's 2015 and 2018 reporting gives a flat "1599 AD" with no source cited in the fetched text — roughly consistent by standard calendar conversion, but framed differently by the two sources. (3) On the site's current physical state: Qaiser (1998, pre-dating the Dawn reporting) already describes it reduced to a small garden with shops; Dawn (2015) describes "a mere small opening in an open space" with residual well access; Dawn (2018) separately flags "the knocking down of the Gurdwara at Baoli Sahib" as an unaddressed grievance, implying a further demolition beyond the baoli itself. None of these three conflicts is resolved here.

Description:
Gurdwara Chakki Sahib stands within the old town of Eminabad in Gujranwala District — the settlement known in Guru Nanak's day as Saidpur — and marks the place where a great millstone (*chakki*) associated with the Guru was kept. It commemorates one of the most dramatic episodes of Guru Nanak's life: his imprisonment during the invasion of the Punjab by the Mughal *Babur*, traditionally dated to around 1520-21, when Eminabad was sacked and its people carried off. According to Sikh tradition the captives, Guru Nanak among them, were set to grinding corn with hand-mills to feed the conquering army; and it is remembered that the Guru's millstone turned of its own accord while he, pouring in the grain, sang the praises of the One God — the hymns lamenting the horrors visited upon the land that are preserved in Sikh scripture as the *Babar-vani*, the "utterances concerning Babur." The marvel is said to have astonished his guards and, when reported to Babur, to have brought the emperor himself to the Guru; moved by his words, Babur is remembered to have sought his blessing and, at the Guru's urging, to have freed many prisoners. The present shrine, a simple flat-roofed building within a brick-paved compound, preserves the memory of the millstone and of the Guru's witness against the cruelty of war. Since Partition it has stood without a resident congregation, cared for as part of Pakistan's Sikh heritage and visited by pilgrims on the great anniversaries, often together with the neighbouring Eminabad shrines of Rori Sahib and Bhai Lalo's well.

Iqbal Qaiser's 1998 survey records that fourteen *ghumaon* of land remain attached to the shrine, that two rooms surviving from Babur's own period still stand within it, and that a fair is held here at Visakhi, with the *Nishan Sahib* flying in the courtyard; the Encyclopaedia of Sikhism further notes that the shrine was administered by the Shiromani Gurdwara Parbandhak Committee from 28 February 1922 until 1947, and that a hymn of Guru Nanak's preserved in the Guru Granth Sahib is read as evidence that he was himself present at Eminabad when Babur sacked it. Visiting in 2017, the journalist Haroon Khalid found the gurdwara's wooden door locked, the building identified only by a small plaque reading “Gurudwara Chakki Sahib, Eimanabad.”

## Bibliography
- Khan Mohammad Waliullah Khan, *Sikh Shrines in West Pakistan*, Memoir of the Department of Archaeology in Pakistan No. 3 (Department of Archaeology, Government of Pakistan, 1962), entry 2, Gujranwala District.
- Iqbal Qaiser, *Historical Sikh Shrines in Pakistan* (Punjabi History Board, 1998), p. 56.
- "Eminabad," in *The Encyclopaedia of Sikhism*, Vol. II: E–L, ed. Harbans Singh, 3rd ed. (Punjabi University, Patiala, 2011).
- Haroon Khalid, "A visit to Gujranwala's Eimanabad throws new light on Babur's legacy," *Dawn*, 4 January 2017.
qa_note: Sources disagree on the date of Babur's sack of Saidpur/Eminabad: Iqbal Qaiser, *Historical Sikh Shrines in Pakistan* (1998), p. 56, dates the capture to “Samvat 1578” without a Gregorian conversion, while the Encyclopaedia of Sikhism's entry on Eminabad states the town “was sacked by Babar in 1521.” The sources also frame Guru Nanak's release slightly differently — the 1962 Department of Archaeology memoir has Babur personally holding a discourse with the Guru before freeing all of Saidpur's captives, while Qaiser's account emphasises the officials reporting the miracle up the chain. Neither discrepancy is resolved here.

Description:
Gurdwara Chhevin Patshahi stands in the small village of Chitti Gatti, in a garden by the roadside about eight kilometres from Mansehra in the Hazara hills of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa. Its name — Chhevin Patshahi, the "Sixth Sovereignty" — commemorates Guru Hargobind, the sixth Guru of the Sikhs (Guru from 1606 to 1644), who by tradition is said to have visited the site during his travels through the region. The gurdwara is a handsomely built, domed structure, and it is remembered above all for an unusual arrangement of shared sacred use: a stone Shiv Ling was worshipped on the upper floor of the building while the prakash of the Guru Granth Sahib was installed on the floor below, with Hindu priests officiating — an arrangement that reflects the closely intertwined Hindu and Sikh devotion of the frontier, where the Guru was honoured by Hindus and Sikhs alike. A fair was traditionally held here at Vaisakhi, enthusiastically attended by the communities of the surrounding hills. The building stands beside the Shiv Mandir of Chitti Gatti (recorded separately in this dataset), the two shrines together forming a single sacred spot. Following the Partition of 1947 the Sikh and Hindu populations of the area departed and regular worship ceased, though the structure survives as a monument to the region's plural religious past.

This account rests on Iqbal Qaiser's 1998 survey, which describes the gurdwara as “beautifully constructed,” with a stone Shiv Ling still in place on the upper floor where it once shared devotion with the Guru Granth Sahib below; the site is also entered in the Department of Archaeology's 1962 register of Sikh shrines in West Pakistan as a “Gurdwara Chitti Chatti” in Hazara district near Mansehra, illustrated there by a photograph captioned “Gurdwara at Mansehra.”

## Bibliography
- Iqbal Qaiser, *Historical Sikh Shrines in Pakistan* (Punjabi History Board, 1998), p. 228.
- Khan Mohammad Waliullah Khan, *Sikh Shrines in West Pakistan*, Memoir of the Department of Archaeology in Pakistan No. 3 (Department of Archaeology, Government of Pakistan, 1962), Appendix 2, "List of the Shrines."
qa_note:
coordinates are adjacent to the Shiv Mandir Chiti Ghati (row 69) and are approximate; the two sites are co-located at Chitti Gatti. Distinct from the Gurdwara Chhevin Patshahi at Hadiara in Lahore district.

This addition rests primarily on a single independently-verified source (Iqbal Qaiser, 1998) for its descriptive detail; the only other citable source found, the 1962 Department of Archaeology register, merely lists and locates the site without independently corroborating the description, so this has not yet been corroborated by a second full account. Note also: press coverage of a 2021 restoration of “a Sikh gurdwara in Mansehra district” (Tribune India, 10 July 2021) concerns a different, unrelated site — Sri Guru Singh Sabha, founded in 1905 — and must not be confused with this Guru-Hargobind-era shrine at Chitti Gatti.

Description:
Gurdwara Chhevin Patshahi at Jhalian — a village of the Lahore District lying in the former Barki (Burki) police-station area, some five kilometres east of Barki town and close to the Lahore–India borderland — commemorates a visit by Guru Hargobind, the sixth Guru (*Chhevin Patshahi*). The settlement is paired with the neighbouring village of Dhilwan, the two together being known as *Jhalian Dhilwan*. By Sikh tradition the Guru halted here and blessed the local *sangat*, and it was from this place, the accounts hold, that he afterwards travelled the short distance to Hadiara, where another gurdwara of the sixth Guru still stands (a separate entry in this dataset). The shrine at Jhalian is remembered as a modest but dignified building raised over the spot said to have been "touched by the feet" of Guru Hargobind: constructed in the manner of a colonial-era bungalow, with a verandah across the front and two rooms behind, and endowed by the villagers with some eight *ghumaon* of land for its upkeep. Like the great majority of gurdwaras on the Pakistani side of the 1947 border, it was maintained by the local Sikh community until Partition, after which the congregation departed and the building passed out of regular worship — such border-village shrines being frequently left empty or turned to other uses thereafter. Its history survives chiefly in Sikh pilgrimage literature and gazetteers rather than in independent record, and its present condition is not well documented. It should not be confused with the other shrines of the sixth Guru in the Lahore region — among them the *Chhevin Patshahi* gurdwaras at Mozang and inside Bhati Gate within Lahore city, and the one at Chitti Gatti near Mansehra recorded elsewhere in this dataset — each marking a different halt in Guru Hargobind's travels.

Iqbal Qaiser's 1998 survey adds that a refugee family from Ambala had settled in the Jhalian building, and that at Dhilwan a *Manji Sahib* — the seat marking where Guru Hargobind himself sat, reached from Jhalian after he had visited many other villages — stood east of the village, its former place of *prakash* now adjoined by a primary school. Independent record of the Guru's route between the two villages appears in the Department of Archaeology's 1962 survey of Sikh shrines in West Pakistan, which lists a “Gurdwara at Dhisalwan, Police Station Barki” under a variant spelling of Dhilwan.

## Bibliography
- Iqbal Qaiser, *Historical Sikh Shrines in Pakistan* (Punjabi History Board, 1998), pp. 276, 278.
- Khan Mohammad Waliullah Khan, *Sikh Shrines in West Pakistan*, Memoir of the Department of Archaeology in Pakistan No. 3 (Department of Archaeology, Government of Pakistan, 1962), entry 6, Lahore District.

Gurdwara Choa Sahib — its name meaning the "gurdwara of the exalted spring" — stands at the northern edge of the great sixteenth-century *Rohtas Fort*, a UNESCO World Heritage Site near Jhelum, close to the fort's Talaqi gate. It commemorates a tradition of *Guru Nanak* (1469–1539): Sikhs hold that the Guru, travelling with his companion *Bhai Mardana* during the fourth of his great journeys (*udasis*) and having spent forty days at the nearby *Tilla Jogian*, came to this waterless tract in the heat of summer. When Bhai Mardana lamented his thirst, the Guru is said to have struck the ground with his staff and moved a stone, causing a natural spring to well up — the *choa* that gives the shrine its name. A further Sikh legend relates that Sher Shah Suri, builder of Rohtas Fort, thrice attempted to divert the spring uphill to supply his stronghold, and thrice his engineers failed. The first commemorative structure, with a *sarovar* (sacred tank) and a place for the recitation of the *Guru Granth Sahib*, is attributed to Charat Singh; the present building dates from 1834 and was commissioned by *Maharaja Ranjit Singh*. Long neglected after the Partition of 1947, the gurdwara was reopened to pilgrims around the time of Guru Nanak's 550th birth anniversary in 2019, and from 2020 a diaspora Sikh organisation undertook its rehabilitation and restoration.

Iqbal Qaiser's 1998 survey adds that Maharaja Ranjit Singh endowed the shrine with twenty-seven *ghumaon* of land and Rs 260, and that a fair was held here on the fifteenth of *Kattak Suddi*. In January 2019 a delegation of the Walled City of Lahore Authority, led by Director General Kamran Lashari, inspected the gurdwara together with the nearby Janam Asthan Mata Sahib Kaur and directed the local administration to restore both sites; that August, seventy-two years after Partition, the Evacuee Trust Property Board formally reopened Gurdwara Choa Sahib for worship, its chairman Dr Aamer Ahmed presiding over a ceremony open to Sikh pilgrims “whether they come from India or any other part of the world.”

## Bibliography
- Iqbal Qaiser, *Historical Sikh Shrines in Pakistan* (Punjabi History Board, 1998), p. 178.
- "WCLA to help restore Sikh sites in Jhelum," *Dawn*, 2 January 2019.
- "72 years after Partition, Pak opens Gurdwara Choa Sahib for Sikh devotees," *The Tribune* (Chandigarh), 2 August 2019.
- "A Complete Tour Guide To Ghurdwara Choa Sahib, Pakistan," Ministry of Religious Affairs and Interfaith Harmony, Government of Pakistan (text closely mirrors the English Wikipedia article "Gurdwara Chowa Sahib").
qa_note: Sources disagree on which gate of Rohtas Fort the gurdwara stands near: Iqbal Qaiser, *Historical Sikh Shrines in Pakistan* (1998), p. 178, places it “outside Kabuli Darwaza (gate),” while the Ministry of Religious Affairs and Interfaith Harmony's page (whose wording closely mirrors the English Wikipedia article and should be read as corroboration of the standard account rather than independent research) places it “near the fort's Talaqi gate” — the gate named in this entry's Description above. The two are not reconciled here.

Description:
Gurdwara Khoohi Bhai Lalo, in the old town of Eminabad, marks the home and the narrow well (*khooi*) of *Bhai Lalo*, the honest carpenter with whom *Guru Nanak Dev Ji* lodged when he came to the town in the early sixteenth century. Bhai Lalo, traditionally said to have been born at Saidpur (Eminabad) in 1452 into a family of carpenters, became one of the most beloved of the Guru's early companions, and his house grew into a *dharamsala*, a gathering-place for the local followers of Guru Nanak. The site is inseparable from one of the most famous of all the *sakhis*: the story of *Malik Bhago*, a wealthy official of Eminabad who held a great feast and was affronted when the Guru chose the plain fare of the labouring carpenter over his own rich table. Summoned to explain himself, Guru Nanak is remembered to have taken Bhai Lalo's coarse bread in one hand and Malik Bhago's fine bread in the other and pressed them: from the honest man's bread there flowed milk, and from the oppressor's, blood — a sign, the Guru explained, that Lalo's food was earned by the sweat of honest toil, while Bhago's was wrung from the exploitation of the poor. The parable of the milk and the blood has ever since stood at the heart of the Sikh ethic of *kirat karni*, of earning one's bread by honest labour and sharing it with others. The gurdwara, named for the well that still survives, preserves this memory; since Partition it has been maintained as part of Pakistan's Sikh heritage and visited by pilgrims, usually in the same round as the nearby Chakki Sahib and Rori Sahib shrines.

Iqbal Qaiser's 1998 survey identifies Bhai Lalo as “a carpenter of *Getaura* caste” whose house, once Guru Nanak had lodged there, was made into a gurdwara remembered as Bhai Lalu Di Khoi, the well from which the Guru had drunk still preserved within it. The same source records that a refugee family occupied the building after 1947 until 1989, when Sardar Surjit Singh Panesar purchased and restored it with funds raised by the Sangat abroad, at which time the well was covered over with a platform.

## Bibliography
- Iqbal Qaiser, *Historical Sikh Shrines in Pakistan* (Punjabi History Board, 1998), pp. 58-60.
- District Gujranwala, Government of Punjab, "Important Places," official district website, accessed 16 August 2026.
qa_note: The official Gujranwala district government's “Important Places” page attributes Eminabad's Bhai-Lalo tradition to a differently-named neighbouring shrine, Gurdwara Rori Sahib, rather than to Khoohi Bhai Lalo specifically; Iqbal Qaiser's 1998 survey treats the two as separate structures, and this entry does not resolve which gurdwara the tradition most properly belongs to. The slug's spelling “Khooi” also differs from Qaiser's “Khoi” and the more common web rendering “Khuhi” — attested alternate transliterations of the same Punjabi word for “well,” not necessarily different places. This addition rests on a single independently-verified source (Qaiser 1998) for its descriptive and restoration detail and has not yet been corroborated by a second independent account specific to this site.

Description:
Gurdwara Patshahi Chhevin at Hadiara, a village of the Lahore District lying off the Lahore–Ghawindi (formerly Lahore–Patti) road near the Bambawali–Ravi–Bedian (BRB) canal, commemorates a visit by Guru Hargobind, the sixth Guru (*Chhevin Patshahi*). By tradition the Guru — *Miri–Piri da Malik*, "master of the temporal and the spiritual" — came to Hadiara with a body of Sikhs around 1620 and stayed overnight to bless the local *sangat*. Before Partition the gurdwara held a large annual fair at *Maghi*, and in the days of the Sikh Empire it is said to have been endowed with some hundred acres of land; it was administered by the Shiromani Gurdwara Parbandhak Committee until 1947. After Partition the shrine fell empty and was for a time occupied by refugees; during the 1965 war soldiers of the Indian Army's Sikh Regiment, reaching the border village, are reported to have repaired its shell-damaged dome and raised a *Nishan Sahib* upon it. The building, the tallest in Hadiara, survives with notable interior murals depicting episodes of Sikh history, including the Battle of Kartarpur of 1635. It should not be confused with the Gurdwara Chhevin Patshahi at Chitti Gatti near Mansehra (a separate entry in this dataset), which commemorates the same Guru at a different place. This account is corroborated by Iqbal Qaiser's on-the-ground survey of Sikh shrines in Pakistan, which independently confirms Guru Hargobind's visit "in recognition of the affection of the Sikh Sangat," describes the gurdwara as "the tallest building of the village," and records that by the time of his survey it was occupied specifically by refugees from Amritsar.

## Bibliography
- Iqbal Qaiser, *Historical Sikh Shrines in Pakistan* (Lahore: Punjabi History Board, 1998), p. 283–284.
qa_note: Non-conflation warning: widely-reported press coverage of a Lahore-district gurdwara "reopened after 79 years" in July 2026 (Tribune India, 11 July 2026, "Historic gurdwara linked to Guru Hargobind reopens in Lahore after 79 years") concerns a different site — Gurdwara Patshahi Chhevin at Amar Sidhu, on the Lahore–Kasur road, rebuilt in 1923 through the efforts of Bhai Mohan Singh Akali (Nihang) — not this Hadiara gurdwara. Iqbal Qaiser's *Historical Sikh Shrines in Pakistan* (1998) lists Amar Sadhu/Amar Sidhu as a distinct entry immediately following its Hadiara entry, and the Wikipedia article specific to this Hadiara gurdwara (matching the sheet's coordinates) makes no mention of any 2026 reopening. This addition rests on a single independently-verified source (Qaiser) and has not yet been corroborated by a second source.

Description:
Gurdwara Pehli Patshahi, popularly called Jind Pir, stands on the Sukkur side of the great bridge that carries the Lahore–Karachi railway across the Indus between Sukkur and Rohri. By tradition it marks a spot graced by Guru Nanak, the first Guru (*Pehli Patshahi*), during his third journey (*udasi*) through Sindh; it was from here, the tradition holds, that he crossed to the river islet later famous as Sadh Belo (a separate entry in this dataset). Its first custodian is said to have been an Udasi *sadhu* of the Jhulelal devotion, and the shrine passed into the keeping of the Nanakpanthi community of Sindh — Hindus and Sikhs together — who honour Guru Nanak without a firm confessional boundary. Within, the *Guru Granth Sahib* is installed and its *prakash* performed, while images are also venerated, and a lamp said to have been kindled by the Guru himself is kept burning day and night, before which pilgrims bow. The gurdwara is thus a characteristic monument of Sindh's syncretic Nanakpanthi tradition, distinct both from the island temple of Sadh Belo and from the other Sikh sites of the Sukkur–Rohri conurbation. Much of its detailed history survives only in oral and community tradition. Independent, gazetteer-derived scholarship attests that the name "Zinda Pir" (or "Jinda Pir") also belongs to an older riverine shrine at Sukkur, at which Hindus and Muslims worshipped jointly until the late nineteenth century, when — per the 1919 Gazetteer of Sindh — the Hindu congregation "abandoned their claim and set up a shrine of their own to Jinda Pir on the Sukkur bank"; whether that shrine and this Sikh gurdwara are the same structure, two structures sharing one name, or otherwise related is not established by any source consulted, and neither account confirms the other.

## Bibliography
- Iqbal Qaiser, *Historical Sikh Shrines in Pakistan* (Lahore: Punjabi History Board, 1998), p. 120.
- Alice Albinia, "Life Around The Indus: Tracing River Worship In Sindh," *Outlook Traveller*, 30 September 2014.
qa_note: Open question, not resolved: Iqbal Qaiser's *Historical Sikh Shrines in Pakistan* places this gurdwara ("Gurdwara Pehli Patshahi, Jind Pir") on the Sukkur side of the bridge, in Nanakpanthi Hindu keeping. Alice Albinia's account (via the 1874 and 1919 Gazetteers of Sindh, in *Outlook Traveller*, 2014) independently describes a similarly-named "Zinda Pir"/"Jinda Pir" shrine on an Indus islet at Sukkur, historically shared by Hindus and Muslims, with the Hindu congregation later founding a shrine of their own on the Sukkur bank — geographically consistent with where Qaiser places the gurdwara, but Albinia's account makes no mention of Sikhs, Guru Nanak, or a gurdwara at all. Whether the two sources describe the same physical site is unresolved and reported here rather than decided. This addition rests on a single independently-verified source for the gurdwara itself (Qaiser) and has not yet been corroborated by a second source that confirms the Sikh gurdwara specifically.

Description:
The Sikh gurdwara at Saidpur Village stands at the foot of the Margalla Hills on the northern edge of Islamabad, within the historic multi-faith village that also preserves a Hindu temple complex (the Ram Kund mandirs). Saidpur is an old settlement — traditionally traced to the early sixteenth century and named after Sultan Said Khan, a chief of the Pothohar region — that served in Mughal times as a garden resort watered by its perennial springs, and that long sheltered a mingled population of Hindus, Sikhs, and Muslims. The gurdwara was built by the Sikh community in the early twentieth century and is remembered as having housed a school dedicated to the teachings of Guru Nanak, the founder of the Sikh faith. It remained active until the Partition of 1947, after which, the Sikh congregation having departed, the building was repurposed — for a time as a girls' school — before being closed in the mid-2000s when Saidpur was developed as a cultural-heritage and tourist village by the Capital Development Authority. Standing beside the temples and close to an old mosque, the disused gurdwara is today valued chiefly as a monument to the religious plurality of pre-Partition Saidpur, a small but eloquent survival of the shared life of the Pothohar. This is the Saidpur Village of Islamabad's Margalla Hills — confirmed against the sheet's coordinates, which match this dataset's separate Ram Mandir, Saidpur entry — and is not to be confused with the historical Saidpur that is an alternate name for Eminabad in Gujranwala District, a distinct place described in other Sikh-shrine literature. Press coverage describes the gurdwara's construction only as "probably" twentieth-century, without a firmer date, and notes its bright yellow domes standing beside the temple complex, with the attached schoolroom serving as a base for teaching the philosophy of Guru Nanak.

## Bibliography
- The Express Tribune (APP), "Antiquity of Saidpur Village lures tourists," 28 December 2020.
- Aamir Saeed, "In Pakistani capital, a centuries-old temple where Hindus are not allowed to pray," Arab News PK, 7 July 2020 (updated 8 July 2020).
qa_note: Neither of the two independent press sources verified for this entry — The Express Tribune (2020) and Arab News PK (2020) — ties Guru Nanak personally to this gurdwara; both describe it only as built "probably" in the twentieth century by the Sikh community, with an attached school dedicated to Guru Nanak's teachings, and neither gives a specific founding year or builder. The dedication implied by this entry's name ("Guru Nanak Dev Ji") is therefore reported as unsubstantiated by the sources found, not resolved. This addition also confirms the entry's location as Saidpur Village, Islamabad (33.7425, 73.0671) — the same coordinates as this dataset's Ram Mandir, Saidpur entry — and not the historical Saidpur that is an alternate name for Eminabad, Gujranwala District, referenced in Sikh-shrine literature such as Iqbal Qaiser's survey; the two should not be conflated. This entry's verdict is PARTIAL: while the two press sources corroborate each other on the gurdwara's existence and rough dating, they leave the Guru Nanak connection and the precise founding date unverified.

Description:
Gurdwara Sri Tilganji Sahib stands on Masjid Road in the heart of Quetta, the capital of Balochistan. By Sikh tradition the site marks a visit by Guru Nanak, the first Guru, during one of his great journeys, or udasis: it is said that the Guru honoured the assembled sangat by distributing til — sesame seeds — as parshad, the sanctified offering, and that from this the shrine took its name, Tilganji deriving from til (sesame) and ganj (treasury or store). The gurdwara is a substantial domed building whose main gateway is said to resemble that of a mosque; within its precincts, in a pattern common to many gurdwaras in Pakistan after 1947, a government school — the Government Sandeman School — has long functioned, occupying land belonging to the shrine. Quetta was almost entirely destroyed in the catastrophic earthquake of 1935, so that the present fabric of the building, like much of the city, is unlikely to be of great antiquity, even if the sanctity of the site is older. The gurdwara is one of the principal Sikh shrines of the city and is to be distinguished from the Gurdwara Singh Sabha of Quetta, recorded separately in this dataset. Iqbal Qaiser's 1998 survey of Sikh shrines in Pakistan records that, in addition to the Sandeman School already functioning within the shrine's precincts, a new government school building had by then been constructed on vacant land belonging to the gurdwara, and that the Sangat of Quetta had filed suit in the lower courts seeking to recover possession of the property.

## Bibliography
- Iqbal Qaiser, *Historical Sikh Shrines in Pakistan* (Lahore: Punjabi History Board, 1998), p. 134.
qa_note:
coordinates approximate (central Quetta, Masjid Road area); distinct from row 88 Gurdwara Singh Sabha. Founding predates the 1935 earthquake; structural age hedged accordingly.

This addition rests on a single independently-verified source (Iqbal Qaiser's 1998 survey) and has not yet been corroborated by a second independent source; no other citable account of the Sandeman School dispute or the gurdwara's legal status was located in this research pass. The source consulted here neither confirms nor contradicts the sheet's year_built/year_built_note (circa 1940, rebuilt after the 1935 Quetta earthquake), which remains unverified against the record found.

Description:
On Lytton Road in Old Anarkali, directly opposite the Anarkali station of the Orange Line Metro Train, stands the Jain Mandir, one of the last physical reminders of Lahore's once-substantial Jain community. Built around 1940 to serve the city's Bhabra Jain merchant families — Punjab having historically been home to a significant Jain trading population — the temple follows a shikhara-style form typical of North Indian Jain architecture and was dedicated to the veneration of the Tirthankaras, the enlightened teacher-figures central to Jain belief and practice. Like much of Lahore's pre-Partition religious minority heritage, the temple fell into disuse after 1947, when the great majority of the city's Jain and Hindu population departed for India. Its most severe blow came in 1992, when it was heavily vandalised in retaliation for the demolition of the Babri Masjid in Ayodhya, India, leaving the building damaged and effectively abandoned for three decades. The turning point came in December 2021, when Pakistan's Supreme Court ordered its restoration, leading to an eight-month conservation effort. The temple reopened in June 2022, allowing religious use to resume after a hiatus of roughly thirty years — an unusual and widely reported instance in Pakistan of an active return to worship, rather than mere heritage preservation, at a minority religious site. Though Jainism has only a residual presence in contemporary Pakistan, the temple's revival has been framed in Pakistani and international press as a significant, if modest, gesture of religious pluralism, and the building today stands as a rare functioning Jain place of worship anywhere in the country, embedded within the dense, historically layered streetscape of Old Anarkali. Independent, established-press reporting adds further precision to this account: Dawn's Sheharyar Rizwan reports that the temple was "constructed by a woman with her own resources in 1940," though her name is not recorded in the surviving coverage, and that after the 1992 attack "the temple's canopy was the only piece of the original structure that survived"; its ruins then lay neglected for over two decades until, in 2016, the remaining site was enclosed behind a boundary wall and the land given away to the Orange Line Metro Train project. The Supreme Court's restoration order, issued in December 2021 by then Chief Justice Gulzar Ahmed, came a day before the nineteenth anniversary of the Babri Masjid's demolition and was reported by the Express Tribune to run alongside a parallel restoration case for Lahore's Neela Gumbad (Blue Tomb); of at least a dozen Jain temples once standing in the city, per Youlin Magazine, this is the sole survivor, and it is not listed among the Punjab Archaeology Department's own "Religious Monuments."

## Bibliography
- Sheharyar Rizwan, "Under-reconstruction Jain Mandir in Lahore all set to reopen," *Dawn*, 1 April 2022.
- "Pakistan set to reopen Lahore's famous Jain temple," *The Express Tribune*, 5 December 2021.
- Muhammad Asif Nawaz, "Story of the Jain Mandir," *Youlin Magazine*, 20 July 2022.
qa_note: Sources disagree slightly on the exact construction period: Dawn (1 April 2022) states the temple was built specifically "in 1940," while Youlin Magazine (20 July 2022) hedges that "it is safe to assume it came about in late 1930s or early 1940s"; neither source names the woman credited with funding its construction, and this is reported rather than resolved. Separately, Dawn's April 2022 report quotes ETPB's Faraz Abbas estimating restoration completion "in just over a month" (around May 2022) with "over 70pc" of work then done; no source verified in this research pass confirms whether that timeline held, so the June 2022 reopening date given elsewhere in this entry is not independently reconfirmed here.

Description:
## Overview

In the Shahi Bazaar of Kalat — the ancient hill-town of central Balochistan that was for centuries the seat of the Khanate of Kalat — stands a Hindu temple dedicated to the goddess Kali. Local tradition holds the shrine to be of great antiquity, with some accounts tracing its origins to the pre-Islamic Sewa dynasty period and claiming an age of some 1,500 years; no dated inscription or independent historical record has been located to confirm so early a founding, and the claim is best treated as devotional tradition rather than settled fact.

## A Living Shrine in a Historic Bazaar

The temple's presence within the working fabric of Kalat's old bazaar reflects a resident Hindu trading community that has occupied the town's commercial life alongside its Baloch and Brahui neighbours, a pattern of minority presence in Balochistan's interior towns that predates the modern state and has persisted, in much reduced form, into the present.

## Festival and Pilgrimage

The temple's clearest claim to wider recognition is its annual three-day Kali festival, held each January, which draws Hindu pilgrims from across Pakistan and, on occasion, from India — a notable instance of cross-border devotional travel to a small provincial shrine.

Independent confirmation of the temple's antiquity comes from the colonial-era *Ethnographic Survey of Baluchistan* (1913), which records the Kalat shrine as "probably the oldest place of Hindu worship" in the region and describes a perpetual lamp, or *jōt*, kept burning day and night, its oil historically supplied by the state itself. Press coverage of the temple's 2023 festival reports that it houses the second-largest Kali statue in Asia, and a 2017 profile found its rites then led by a young priest, Maharaj Sain Shamgir, before a congregation of about 35 worshippers, with Kalat city's own Hindu population put at some 200 households — of an estimated 100 families who had migrated elsewhere, roughly 80 were reported to have since returned. That same 2017 account also recorded a local priest's tradition that the city of Kalat itself takes its name from a Hindu ruler he called "Kalat Seva" — a separate oral tradition, distinct from the Sewa-dynasty founding narrative above, and not independently corroborated.

## Bibliography

- Wikipedia, "Kali Temple, Kalat."
- Local and regional press coverage of the annual Kalat Kali festival.
- Denys Bray, *Ethnographic Survey of Baluchistan*, Vol. 2 (Bombay: The Times Press, 1913).
- Muhammad Akbar Notezai, "Footprints: Descendants of Royalty," *Dawn*, 15 October 2017.
- "Three-day annual festival starts at Kalat's Kali Mandir," Associated Press of Pakistan, *The Express Tribune*, 24 January 2023.
qa_note: The addition above draws on a colonial-era ethnographic survey (Bray, 1913) and established press coverage (Dawn, 2017; The Express Tribune, 2023), but the underlying research pass is rated PARTIAL: the founding-date and dynasty claims already carried in this Description (the Sewa-dynasty origin and 1,500-year age, above) remain unconfirmed against any source that could be directly fetched, and are retained here only as devotional tradition. The newly-added claim that "Kalat" derives from a Hindu ruler called "Kalat Seva" rests on a single 2017 press interview with a local priest and has not been cross-checked against Bray or any other source — it should be read as a second, likewise unresolved, naming tradition, not as confirmed history.

Description:
The Khatwari Darbar is among the most celebrated of the historic Sikh and Nanakpanthi shrines of Shikarpur, the north-Sindh town once known as the "Paris of Sindh" for the wealth of its merchant houses. It is traditionally held to have been founded by Bhai Gurdas Singh — also remembered by the name Kanhiya Lal — a disciple of Guru Gobind Singh who, after the Guru's death in 1708, is said to have travelled to Sindh and preached the Sikh teaching at Shikarpur. He is remembered as delivering his sermons seated upon a *khat* (a rope cot), from which the darbar took its name, "Khatwari". The building most likely dates to the second quarter of the eighteenth century and is one of the finest structures in the town: a two-storey *haveli*-style darbar noted for its fresco paintings and intricate woodwork, decoration rarely matched elsewhere in upper Sindh. Images of the ten Sikh Gurus adorn its walls, and three doorways open onto the main hall, where the *Guru Granth Sahib* is installed. The darbar belongs to the shared Nanakpanthi and *Udasi* devotional world of Sindh, in which Sindhi Hindus and Sikhs venerated the Gurus together. There are in fact three Khatwari Darbars in Shikarpur — the principal one, or Khatwari Dharamshala, in Thekrati Bazar — and the tradition of Bhai Gurdas is also remembered at Shahdadkot and at Gandava in Jhal Magsi.

Local tradition, as recorded by the anthropologist Zulfiqar Ali Kalhoro, adds a specific origin story: Guru Gobind Singh is said to have found Bhai Gurdas serving water to wounded Muslim and Sikh soldiers alike, and instructed him to carry the teaching to Shikarpur. The darbar's hall houses, alongside the *Guru Granth Sahib*, an image of Sri Chand — Guru Nanak's eldest son — and the *Jyot*, or sacred light, of Jhulelal, binding the shrine into Sindh's wider devotional world. The building was originally five storeys and is now reduced to two; its two entrances carry marble images of Durga and of Ganpati flanked by his two wives, and its central door bears ten carved panels of Sikh Gurus and saints, including Baba Sewa Das and Baba Kashi Das. By 2018 its mural paintings were reported in advanced decay and its ornate wooden doors sold off to dealers, and the darbar's once-extensive precinct has shrunk to a few buildings, with its former Vidyalaya now rebuilt as a charity hospital; a branch was also established in Mumbai after Partition. The darbar's continued existence and its housing of the Guru Granth Sahib were independently confirmed in 2013, when it was named among Sindh shrines hit by a wave of reported desecrations.

## Bibliography

- Zulfiqar Ali Kalhoro, "The Magnificent Khatwari Darbar in Shikarpur," *Youlin Magazine*, 6 June 2024.
- Zulfiqar Ali Kalhoro, "Gurus in Shikarpur," *The Friday Times*, 12 January 2018.
- Staff Reporter, "Desecration of Guru Granth Sahib across Sindh cities slammed," *Dawn*, 28 August 2013.
qa_note: The addition above draws on two articles by the anthropologist Zulfiqar Ali Kalhoro (The Friday Times, 2018; Youlin Magazine, 2024) and an independent 2013 Dawn report confirming the darbar's existence and its housing of the Guru Granth Sahib. Several points remain unresolved across the sources: Kalhoro's own two articles spell the founder's original name differently ("Kanhiya Lal" in 2024 vs "Kanya Lal" in 2018); the 2024 article records an alternative tradition that Bhai Gurdas first preached at Gandava in Balochistan, not Shikarpur; and a Wikipedia passage (not independently verified) describes the darbar as dedicated to Bhai Kanhaiya, the Sewapanthi founder, whose water-carrier story is similar to but distinct from the one told here of Bhai Gurdas — the relationship between the two figures could not be resolved in this research pass. The detailed architectural and biographical material rests substantially on Kalhoro's own scholarship; only the darbar's bare existence and its housing of the Guru Granth Sahib have independent corroboration.

Description:
The Lal Kurti Temple — also called the *Balmiki* (Valmiki) Mandir — stands in the historic Lalkurti quarter of Rawalpindi Cantonment, a bazaar district whose name ("red shirt") recalls the red tunics of the British Indian Army soldiers who once shopped there and gave the old British Infantry Bazaar its popular name. Completed in 1905 in a Mughal-influenced idiom, the temple is dedicated to the sage-poet *Valmik* (Valmiki), revered as author of the *Ramayana* and venerated especially by the Balmiki community. It remained a focal point for local Hindus both before and after the Partition of 1947; while most of the quarter's Hindus left in 1947, a small community stayed on and kept the temple in worship, and its first post-Partition custodian, Kheera Lal, is buried within a side portion of the complex. As of 2025 it is reported to be the only Hindu place of worship still functioning in Lalkurti — a neighbourhood that once held shrines of several faiths — and it is counted as one of the three principal Hindu temples of Rawalpindi district, alongside the Krishna Mandir of Saddar and the Valmiki Swamiji Mandir of Gracy Lines. The temple hosts daily worship and the major festivals of *Diwali*, *Holi* and *Raksha Bandhan*, and its upkeep has been associated with the Pakistan Hindu Balmik Welfare Society and with the few dozen local families who continue to maintain it.

As of 2025, more than 60 Hindus were reported to live in the immediate Lal Kurti locality, within a wider Hindu population of the twin cities estimated at around 6,000. The temple's caretaker, Om Prakash Narain, 80 years old at the time, was also reported to serve as General Secretary of the Pakistan Hindu Balmik Welfare Society and as a member of the District Peace Committee and the Interfaith Harmony Committee. Press coverage is careful to distinguish this temple from a separate, unrelated structure of similar name — the ruined "Guru Balmik Swamiji's Mandir," a triple-storey temple built in 1880 in Rawalpindi's Purana Qila, stripped of its woodwork and now built over with shops — which should not be confused with the active Lal Kurti temple described here.

- Qaiser Shirazi, "Century-old Balmik Temple stands test of time," *The Express Tribune*, 27 August 2025.
- Qaiser Shirazi, "Rawalpindi's Hindu heritage fades," *The Express Tribune*, 16 December 2025.
- Shiraz Hassan, "Lal Kurti – an epitome of religious co-existence," *Dawn*, 21 August 2014.
- "Pindi lit up as Hindus celebrate 'Festival of Lights'," *The Express Tribune*, 1 November 2024.

qa_note: No conflicts were found among the sources drawn on above. The research file underlying this addition flags a distinct, unrelated site of similar name: a ruined "Guru Balmik Swamiji's Mandir," built 1880 in Rawalpindi's Purana Qila, now stripped and built over with shops (Qaiser Shirazi, *The Express Tribune*, 23 January 2023) — this is a separate structure from the active Lal Kurti/Balmiki temple described in this entry and should not be conflated with it.

Description:
Wedged into the narrow space between the western wall of Lahore Fort and the eastern wall of Hazuri Bagh, close to the Alamgiri Gate, stands one of Lahore's most storied yet architecturally modest religious survivals: the Loh, or Lava, Temple. According to Hindu tradition, Lahore takes its name from Lava (also rendered Luv), twin son of Lord Rama and Sita in the Ramayana, who is said to have founded the city — known in Sanskrit as Lavapuri, the "City of Lava" — while his brother Kusha is traditionally credited with founding nearby Kasur. Despite this ancient legendary association, historians including Sir Edward MacLagan date the surviving structure itself to the early nineteenth century, likely built during or shortly after Maharaja Ranjit Singh's conquest of Lahore Fort in 1799, making it a Sikh-period commemorative shrine to an ancient legend rather than an ancient building in its own right. The temple is a simple hexagonal brick structure of interconnected chambers around an inner sanctum, historically topped by a dome that has since been lost; it contains no surviving Ramayana carvings or frescoes, consistent with its comparatively late construction. For much of the twentieth century the temple stood neglected and largely inaccessible within the Fort precincts. Between 2024 and 2026 it underwent careful restoration by the Walled City of Lahore Authority in partnership with the Aga Khan Cultural Service–Pakistan, funded by the United States Ambassadors Fund for Cultural Preservation, alongside related Sikh-era monuments nearby. It reopened to the public on 27 January 2026, drawing renewed attention in both Pakistani and Indian media as a rare, tangible link between Lahore's Hindu mythological heritage and its physical urban fabric, even though it does not currently host regular congregational worship in the manner of Lahore's active mandirs.

Visiting in 2018, a Dawn correspondent found the then-unrestored temple littered with an empty water bottle and marked by graffiti, and noted that neither of the two historians she consulted could say who built the temple, when, what it once housed, or whether it was ever used for worship at all — questions she concluded "we can only speculate" about. The Walled City of Lahore Authority, which now manages the site, describes it in its own materials as "the temple of Raja Loh," a cluster of interconnected, open-to-sky chambers housing a memorial shrine, and frames its restoration as part of a wider effort to showcase the Fort's cross-cultural heritage of Sikh and Hindu temples, Mughal mosques, and British-period structures alongside one another.

## Bibliography

- Sufia Zamir, "Heritage: The Lonely Little Temple," *Dawn*, 14 January 2018.
- "Temple of Loh — a connection between Prince Loh and Lahore," Walled City of Lahore Authority, walledcitylahore.gop.pk.
- "Temple dedicated to Lord Ram's son restored, opens for public in Pakistan's Lahore," PTI, *The Tribune* (Chandigarh), 27 January 2026.
qa_note: Sources disagree on the restoration timeline and are not reconciled here: Dawn (2018) reports the temple then still neglected and litter-strewn; the Walled City of Lahore Authority's own page states the temple "was conserved by the Walled City of Lahore Authority in 2021"; and a January 2026 wire report (PTI/The Tribune, India) describes a conservation project — undertaken with the Aga Khan Cultural Service — as newly "completed" in 2026, while noting the site had earlier undergone only "partial restoration" in 2018. These three dates (a 2018 partial restoration, a 2021 conservation per the WCLA's own page, and a 2026 completion per the 2026 report) all appear in sourced material and are reported here without being resolved into a single timeline. Separately, Dawn (2018) explicitly cautions that no source can confirm who built the temple, when, or whether it was ever actually used for worship — a deeper uncertainty than the Sikh-period-construction-vs-legendary-origin framing already given in this Description's main text.

Description:
Mohra Sharif is a celebrated *khanqah* — a Sufi lodge and spiritual centre — set in a small village in the Murree hills of the Punjab, some distance above Islamabad and Rawalpindi. It is the home of the *Naqshbandi Mujaddidi Qasimiya* order, and takes its name (the "holy village") from its sanctity. The centre was established by *Khwaja Muhammad Qasim Sadiq*, born about 1846 (1263 AH), whose forebears are said to have migrated from Iran and settled in the Rawalpindi district. According to the traditions of the order, he journeyed on foot to the shrine of his spiritual guide, *Khwaja Nizamuddin Aulia* of Kahiyan Sharif in the Neelam Valley of Kashmir, and there received *khilafat* with the instruction to settle at Mohra Sharif. He is said to have undertaken a *chilla* — a forty-day retreat of unbroken devotion — and the stone slab on which he sat throughout is preserved at the shrine as a relic (*tabarruk*). On his death the spiritual seat passed to his son Khwaja Pir Muhammad Zahid Khan, remembered as the first *sajjada nashin* (custodian) of Mohra Sharif, and thence down a line of successors. The khanqah remains an active centre of Naqshbandi devotion, drawing pilgrims especially at its annual *urs*, and is counted among the important Sufi shrines of the northern Punjab.

The khanqah's own historical account names the specific line of succession only broadly gestured at above: Khwaja Pir Muhammad Zahid Khan, the founder's third son and first *sajjada nashin*, is recorded as having died on 9 December 1993; he was followed by Hazrat Khawaja Pir Badshah Sahib, who died on 13 August 2008; and then by Pir Auliya Badshah Farooq Sahib as the third *Sajjada Nasheen*. In January 2026, the German Ambassador to Pakistan, Ina Lepel, visited the khanqah — described in press coverage as a "200-year-old Sufi centre" — and met with its custodian, named in that report as Pir Mujtaba Farooq Gull; a second report of the same visit notes that she spent considerable time at the khanqah's attached madrassa, observing classes and discussing curriculum with students.

Description:
The Ram Mandir at Saidpur — also known as the Ram Kund Mandir — stands in the historic village of Saidpur, set in a fold of the Margalla Hills on the northern edge of Islamabad. A Hindu temple dedicated to *Lord Rama*, it is traditionally dated to the sixteenth century and attributed by some accounts to Raja Man Singh I, the Rajput general of the Mughal emperor Akbar. The site's sanctity is bound to the belief that Rama, with Sita and Lakshmana, passed through this country during the years of exile recounted in the *Ramayana*: the natural springs of the village, fed by the hill streams, were revered as sacred pools, and four of them are traditionally named for Rama, Sita, Lakshmana, and Hanuman. Before Partition, Saidpur was a place of notable interfaith coexistence, home to Muslims, Hindus, and Sikhs together, its skyline holding a mosque, this Hindu temple, and — from the early twentieth century — a Sikh *gurdwara*. After 1947 the temple ceased to function as a place of worship; it was used for a time as a girls' school, and in the 2000s the Capital Development Authority restored Saidpur as a heritage and arts village, conserving the temple's fabric while its idols were removed and its images painted over. The building survives as a protected monument and a popular destination for visitors to Islamabad, though the local Hindu community has not been permitted to resume regular rituals there — a source of continuing appeal by Hindu representatives.

According to *Dawn*'s 2016 reporting, local memory also ties the site to the adjoining Ram Kund pond, where — per the 1893-94 Rawalpindi Gazetteer as cited by that report — an annual fair once drew Hindus from across the district; in 2006 the Capital Development Authority had the by-then-vacated building formally cleared and preserved as a tourist attraction, and visitors have since documented restaurants operating within the complex serving meat dishes, a practice criticised by Hindu commentators as an affront to the site's sanctity. A 2020 report independently corroborated the temple's sixteenth-century dating and confirmed that regular Hindu worship remains barred there.

Because one of its central sourced claims (the gazetteer citation) could not be verified, this addition is treated as PARTIAL rather than STRONG: the builder attribution, the Rama exile legend, the sixteenth-century dating, and the post-1947 secular reuse are corroborated by two independent established-press sources (Dawn 2016, Arab News 2020), but the gazetteer-sourced fair claim is not yet corroborated and should be treated with caution.

Description:
The darbar of Sain Vali Vilayat Rai stands in the *Shivalo* quarter of Kambar (Qambar), the headquarters town of the Qambar–Shahdadkot District of upper Sindh, and is described by the anthropologist Zulfiqar Ali Kalhoro as the largest Nanakpanthi *darbar* in the district. Its founder, Vali Vilayat Rai, was born in 1825 into a prosperous Hindu family of Old Hala; his father, Pratab Rai, had served as a *munshi* (secretary) to the Talpur Mirs of Hyderabad. Vali Vilayat Rai settled first at Larkana and later moved to Kambar, where he chose the then-unpopulated Shivalo locality — remembered as a resort of *yogis*, *sants* and *sadhus* drawn from Kambar, Shahdadkot, Larkana and the surrounding towns — and there established his darbar, raising a great hall in which the *Guru Granth Sahib* was installed. Like the wider body of Sindhi Nanakpanthis, his followers venerate the Hindu deities together with Baba Guru Nanak, his son Baba Sri Chand, and the other Sikh Gurus, so that the darbar belongs at once to Hindu and to Sikh devotional worlds; it is entered here under "Hindu Temple" as the closest of the dataset's three categories, following the convention used for the other Sindhi *sant* darbars in this collection. The darbar and the *samadhi* (memorial shrine) of Vali Vilayat Rai remain at Kambar, and the lineage retains a devotional following, though — as with most Sindhi Hindu shrines — much of the community associated with it now lives in India. The saint is counted among a constellation of nineteenth- and early-twentieth-century Nanakpanthi masters of the Larkana country, among them Swami Dharmdas of Larkana and Bhai Waliram of Digano Mahesar.

According to a hagiographic account recorded by the anthropologist Zulfiqar Ali Kalhoro, Vali Vilayat Rai's turn to spiritual life followed his time as a *tapedar* (village accountant) under British rule: irregularities found in his accounts led to imprisonment, during which he is said to have received a vision of Guru Nanak revealing his own previous incarnation as a yogi; thereafter he is remembered as making an annual pilgrimage to the Sufi shrines of Rohri, Sehwan, and Jhok. The present darbar building, a three-storey structure with ornately carved doors and windows in a colonial idiom, is believed to have been erected in 1887. Leadership passed after his death to Sain Jiwat Singh, who ran a free dispensary for the poor of Kambar until his own death in 1899, and then to Jiwat Singh's chief disciple, Vishandas; a branch of the darbar was later established at Kandivali, Bombay (now Mumbai), in 1960, reflecting the wider migration of Sindhi Hindus after Partition.

Description:
Immediately beside Lahore Fort and the Badshahi Mosque, on the spot where Maharaja Ranjit Singh's body was cremated, stands the samadhi built in his memory — one of the grandest funerary monuments of the Sikh Empire. Ranjit Singh, the "Lion of Punjab," founded and ruled the Sikh Empire from 1801 until his death on 27 June 1839. Construction began the following month under his son Kharak Singh and was largely completed by 1848 under his youngest son, Duleep Singh, with final repairs funded by the British after their 1849 annexation of Punjab. At the monument's heart, beneath a marble pavilion inlaid with pietra dura stonework, a lotus-shaped marble urn holds the Maharaja's ashes, surrounded by smaller urns commemorating the four queens and seven attendants who, according to the custom of sati, died on his funeral pyre. Adjoining smaller samadhis honour his son Kharak Singh and grandson Nau Nihal Singh. Architecturally the building is a striking synthesis of Sikh, Hindu and Islamic idioms: gilded fluted domes and cupolas rise above red sandstone doorways carved with images of Ganesha, Devi and Brahma, while surviving interior frescoes, painted between 1839 and 1849, have been reassessed by modern scholars as a high point of Sikh decorative art. Though formally a samadhi rather than a constituted gurdwara, the site has long functioned as a living place of Sikh devotion: the Guru Granth Sahib was installed and read there for decades after construction, and today it remains an active pilgrimage destination, especially around Ranjit Singh's death anniversary and the spring Vaisakhi season, when Sikh visitors, including delegations from India, gather to pay homage. The Evacuee Trust Property Board administers the site, one of the most visited symbols of Sikh heritage remaining in Pakistan.

Modern scholarship has focused particular attention on the samadhi's ornamental programme: research by the art historian Dr Nadhra Shahbaz Naeem Khan uncovered guardian figures beneath whitewash on the building's eastern facade, though subsequent recoatings have since covered and lost this decoration again. The monument is listed by the Punjab Directorate General of Archaeology among the province's protected religious monuments of the Sikh period.

## Bibliography
- Bushra Shehzad, "Rediscovering our Sikh heritage," *Dawn*, 24 May 2012.
- Directorate General of Archaeology, Government of Punjab, "Religious Monuments" (online monument index), accessed 16 August 2026.
qa_note: A Dunya News feature (15 August 2026) states that "the structure originally served as a baradari where Maharaja Ranjit Singh held royal gatherings before it was converted into a memorial Samadhi" and that it "houses commemorative urns associated with the Maharaja's ashes, while tradition holds that most of his ashes were immersed in the River Ganges." Neither claim is corroborated by the two earlier, more rigorously sourced accounts drawn on above — Syad Muhammad Latif's 1892 *Lahore: Its History, Architectural Remains and Antiquities* and Iqbal Qaiser's 1998 *Historical Sikh Shrines in Pakistan* — both of which describe the building as commissioned only after Ranjit Singh's death, as a mausoleum begun under his son Kharak Singh, and both describe the marble lotus in the central vault as directly covering the Maharaja's ashes on-site, with no mention of a Ganges immersion. This discrepancy is reported here, not resolved. Dunya News also gives a vaguer account of who completed construction ("subsequent Sikh rulers") than Latif's more precise sequence (begun under Kharak Singh, partly executed by Sher Singh, finished only in the later part of Dalip Singh's reign).

Description:
This temple at Chak, a town in Shikarpur district, is dedicated to the memory of Bhagat Kanwar Ram (1885–1939), one of the best-loved Sindhi Hindu saint-singers of the twentieth century. Born in the village of Jarwar in the Sukkur region, he became renowned for his rendition of the *Sur Prabhati*, sung in the early morning; the gramophone company HMV is said to have preserved a number of his devotional songs on record, spreading his fame across Sindh. Revered by Hindus and Muslims alike as a figure of piety and communal harmony, he was assassinated at Ruk railway station in the Sukkur area in November 1939 and is remembered as a martyr. The temple at Chak was raised in his name after his death and was rebuilt in 2006; its main hall holds canopies bearing images of Bhagat Kanwar Ram and of Sant Satram Das, the saint of the *Sacho Satram* tradition with whom his memory is closely linked. In a syncretic touch characteristic of Sindhi devotion, the *Guru Granth Sahib* is also installed within, so that the darbar is honoured by Hindu and Sikh worshippers together. Every year on 2 November his followers gather to mark the anniversary of his martyrdom, both at this shrine and at Ruk station where he was killed.

The temple stands specifically in the Lakhi Ghulam Shah taluka of Shikarpur district, roughly 24 km east of Lakhi Ghulam Shah town. Kanwar Ram — born 13 April 1885 at Tarachand's house in Jarwar, then part of Mirpur Mathelo tehsil, and a disciple of Sant Satram Das (1866-1910) — was also remembered for singing the verses of Sufi poets including Shah Abdul Latif Bhittai, Sachal Sarmast, Sami, and Kabir alongside his own devotional compositions. The Chak temple was first managed by Ladak Mal and his family and, following its 2006 rebuilding, has been maintained by Bal Chand Esrani, Tara Chand Thawani, and Prakash Lal Devani. A separate commemoration, distinct from both the Chak temple and the Ruk station gathering, has also been held at the Institute of Sindhology in Hyderabad, where in 2008 the university's vice-chancellor marked Kanwar Ram's 69th death anniversary by announcing a dedicated Bhagat Kanwar Ram Memorial Corner.

Also worth noting: this entry's existing text places the annual commemoration on 2 November, while both established-press sources used here give 1 November as the date of the murder and of the annual gathering at Ruk Railway Station — a one-day difference noted here rather than silently corrected.

Description:
The town of Raharki (Raherki Sahib) in Ghotki district, in upper Sindh close to the Punjab border, is home to the *Sant Satram Dham* — also known as *Devri Sahib*, and, after the devotional movement it anchors, as *Sacho Satram* — reckoned among the largest and most frequented Hindu shrines in present-day Pakistan. It marks the birthplace of *Satguru* Swami Sai Satramdas Sahib, the revered Sindhi saint born here, according to the tradition, on 25 October 1866. He gave his life to spiritual teaching in the syncretic Sindhi devotional mould, preaching love, humility and service to the destitute, and drawing followers from across Sindh who came to him for blessing and healing; the tradition records that he "left the mortal body" on 25 January 1910. After his passing the *Devri* (shrine) at Raharki grew into the principal seat of his lineage, whose devotees revere a holy text recited at the shrine known as the *Dhuni Sahib*. Today thousands of pilgrims — Sindhi Hindus from Pakistan, India and the diaspora — gather at Raharki, especially each October to mark the saint's birth anniversary, and the site is locally described as one of the biggest temples in the country. A succession of *sants* has continued to lead the community, and the darbar sustains traditions of communal hospitality and worship; the town itself is noted as one where Muslims and Hindus have long lived together. His memory is closely linked with that of Bhagat Kanwar Ram (also recorded in this dataset), with whom the *Sacho Satram* tradition is associated.

According to *Dawn*'s 2012 reporting, the darbar forms a sprawling, multi-acre complex a few kilometres from the Bharchundi Sharif shrine, with an enormous pilgrim hostel under construction and a causeway, funded by the federal government, easing access to the site; caretakers there described a mid-April festival marking the death anniversary of Bhagat Kanwar Ram that draws tens of thousands of visitors, including from Dubai and India. A satellite Sant Satram Dham was separately established in Shikarpur town on 9 October 2000, its own displays acknowledging the Raharki complex as the "principal" *Devri Sahib*. In September 2019 the temple — also referred to in press coverage as the SSD Dham Mandir — was attacked during communal unrest in Ghotki; government and civil-society delegations investigating the violence met community leaders on-site and concluded the attack had been planned the night before, and PPP chairman Bilawal Bhutto-Zardari visited the ransacked temple in its aftermath.
